extracted.intended_audience: ICCV/CVPR conference paper reviewers (computer vision researchers serving as reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for reviewing computer-vision conference submissions (ICCV/CVPR). Covers what to include in reviews, how to assess significance/validity, common mistakes to avoid, ethics, and expectations for review quality and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent, objective, critical, and comprehensive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an independent, objective, critical, and comprehensive review. Key: What is the knowledge advancement in the paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be independent and objective in your assessment; focus on whether the paper advances knowledge. Cover all major aspects (ideas, experiments, theory, writing, data contributions) rather than only a subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain basis of review and recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain clearly the basis of your review and recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide solid justifications for your final recommendation. Read the rebuttal and discussion; state whether and why they change your position. Clear explanations help ACs form final recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess knowledge advancement and audience interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept papers that 'present sufficient knowledge advancement that is well grounded' and 'is of sufficient interest to some CVPR/ICCV audiences who could benefit from it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on concrete knowledge advancement rather than topic popularity. Interest may be to a subcommunity — CVPR/ICCV is inclusive and out-of-scope rejections are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize significance / impact (Highlight / Accept / Reject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify papers by impact: Highlight/Best Paper = major advances that will heavily impact the field; Accept = potential to be significant, useful incremental steps, useful tools, or creative plausible ideas; Reject = unlikely to be significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Best papers (e.g., ResNet, Mask R-CNN) create new capabilities and will be widely used. Incremental work can be acceptable if it meaningfully expands knowledge or provides useful resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific correctness and robustness of evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure results are correct and evaluations are not misleading; avoid accepting papers with wrong or fraudulent results or misleading evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for methodological or experimental flaws that invalidate claims. Misleading evaluation makes comparisons hard and harms follow-up work. Consider whether reported errors actually invalidate the main claimed knowledge advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise summary of the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a concise summary describing the key ideas, experiments, and their significance (preferably in 5-7 sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the problem, whether it is new/why it matters, the key to the solution, main contributions, and whether experiments support the claims. A good summary helps ACs and authors understand your perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear statement of strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear statement of the paper’s strengths: key contributions and why they matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss aspects like novelty, theoretical contribution, experimental validation, writing quality, and data contributions when relevant. Explain why these aspects are valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear statement of weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear statement of the paper’s weaknesses: what aspects most need improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between major flaws that affect accept/reject and minor issues. Provide evidence and specifics rather than blanket assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed rating justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide detailed justification of your rating, weighing the strengths and weaknesses of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how you combined different factors to arrive at the score; make it clear which points drive your accept/reject stance so ACs can act on your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional comments (minor suggestions and corrections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include minor suggestions, questions, corrections, and small improvements to help authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label these as 'minor' so ACs know they are not central to the decision. Include presentation fixes, typos, and small clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest sufficient time & effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the time to do a good review: many experienced reviewers take 2–4 hours per paper; newer reviewers should plan at least 4 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the paper twice, consider related work, look up unfamiliar techniques, and check claims carefully. Poorly justified brief reviews are unhelpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be impartial and avoid bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge each paper on its own merits. There is no global quota or requirement to match pile acceptance rates. Be aware of personal biases and discount author identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving more value to topics close to your own research. If you don't know the authors, do not seek them out (e.g., do not try to de-anonymize via arXiv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific and detailed (no blank assertions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific and detailed in claims; avoid summary judgments like 'not novel' or 'unclear' without evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For prior work, give precise references and explain overlap. Provide concrete examples or evidence for any claim you make about the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional and courteous tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain professionalism: avoid belittling, sarcastic, or overly harsh remarks; use third person ('the authors' or 'the paper') rather than 'you'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat requests for citations to be relevant, not self-promotional; do not ask authors to cite your papers merely to push your work. Proofread and spell-check the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor evaluation depth to paper type
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply different levels of evaluation depending on paper type: proof-of-concept, benchmark results, theory/position pieces, or complex/implausible works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., transformative idea may need only basic proof-of-concept; established problems require thorough benchmark results; extraordinary claims require careful scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be constructive and collaborative
rubrics_metrics.description: Be constructive to the authors and friendly to reviewer colleagues and ACs; suggest how the paper could be improved rather than just criticizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus discussion on technical issues, do not take disagreements personally, and accept that reasonable reviewers may disagree. Help ACs reach decisions by being clear and cooperative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit reviews on time and be responsive in discussions; delays increase workload for colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to ACs/review discussions by deadlines (rebuttal/discussion phases). ACs track reviewer performance and may nominate outstanding reviewers for awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ACs for policy/ethical concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise suspicious ethical/mischief concerns to ACs and PCs rather than policing the paper directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed with the review as usual and flag issues for PCs/ACs to handle policy. If you suspect conflicts of interest, contact Program Chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for fundamental flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a comprehensive check of potential fundamental flaws: Are assumptions/theories mathematically sound? Are experiments scientifically valid? Is the problem trivial? Did the paper miss important prior work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether identified errors invalidate the main knowledge claim. Distinguish between fixable issues and fatal flaws that undermine acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arrogance, ignorance, and inaccuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assert things outside your knowledge, be accurate, and avoid arrogant stances (e.g., 'my way or the highway').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you critique something technical, check the authors' claims carefully; do not state incorrect technical facts. If unsure, say so and suggest checks instead of making definitive but wrong claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure opinions and unsupported claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ungrounded subjective statements (e.g., 'this is not good enough for ICCV 2023') without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground statements with 'because ...' and provide evidence or reasoning for opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the novelty fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept/reject solely based on (lack of) novelty; novelty alone is not sufficient to judge significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many useful contributions are not highly novel but still valuable; conversely, novelty does not guarantee importance. Focus on well-grounded knowledge advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blank assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make empty assertions such as 'This has been done before' without citations and explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide references and explain how/why prior work overlaps. Confine critique to technical content rather than to authors' character or competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid policy entrepreneurism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not impose your personal checklist (e.g., 'you must publish your dataset', 'you must have a theorem') as official policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow common scientific review principles and official conference policies. Focus on whether the paper produces significant knowledge advancement rather than imposing extra requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intellectual laziness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overemphasize a single factor (e.g., beating SOTA) or be unsure in a way that leaves ACs unable to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a comprehensive assessment, and if you find an alleged error, evaluate whether it invalidates the main contribution. Don't rely on shallow heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish major vs minor points in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it clear which raised points are major factors in your decision and which are minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show bad reviews that list many issues without a summary/judgment. Good reviews explicitly identify key reasons for acceptance/rejection and which comments are minor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical handling of submissions and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid conflicts of interest; protect authors’ ideas; do not show submissions to others without permission; do not use ideas from submissions in your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact PCs for conflict clarifications. After the process, destroy all copies of papers, supplementary material, and any evaluation code you wrote.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM / automated text ethics for reviews (ICCV ’23 new item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must provide comments that faithfully represent their original opinions; it is unethical to resort to Large Language Models to automatically generate reviewing comments that do not originate from the reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are required to confirm that each review reflects their original opinions and that no parts were generated by an automatic system (e.g., ChatGPT).
